newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: U.S. Congress to push for Asian military presence.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Congress to push for Asian military presence.

text.p: The Republican-led U.S. Congress will push the Clinton administration to keep 100,000 soldiers in Asia as guarantors of stability in the region, a senior congressman said on Friday.

But Douglas Bereuter, a Republican who heads the House of Representatives foreign affairs subcommittee on the region, told the World Economic Forum the U.S. presence and its Asian defence ties were not designed to contain China, an emerging superpower.
"The 100,000-person commitment to the region is not one that will be challenged by Congress," he told a seminar on Asian security at the gathering of business and political leaders.
"Indeed, Congress will probably push the administration to maintain 100,000 even though the capacity under military modernisation might not insist on having 100,000 people there."
Bereuter dismissed suggestions that Washington's reinforced defence ties with its key regional ally Japan and other Pacific nations marked an effort to hem in China's burgeoning might.

"This containment policy is a figment (of the imagination) of people in the media and certain politicans and should not be taken seriously by the Chinese military or the Chinese people," he said, adding Washington and Beijing were not doomed to clash.

"We don't have to be adversaries. That is not in the cards. But it could be tipped in that direction unless it is carefully managed by the U.S., by China working at it as well, and indeed by all of China's neighbours."

Bereuter said Hong Kong's handover to Beijing on July 1 would be a crucial test of how relations developed in the region and go far to determine whether the U.S. "one-China" policy could be sustained amid attacks even from within Congress.

Foreign and defence ministers from the region agreed during a panel discussion that the U.S. military presence was a key factor in heading off potential tension as economic growth financed military build-ups and spurred competition for energy.
But they also suggested Russia had a bigger role to play in the region as Moscow found its feet after the rough transition to free-market democracy.
"Once Russia...becomes a driving economic force again and once it has a greater degree of self-confidence...Russia will want to be more active," Australian Foreign Minister Alexander Downer said.
Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin told a news conference in Davos on Thursday that Moscow wanted to join the Asian Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum.

"I think it is wrong to ignore Russia just because it is preoccupied at the moment, let us say euphemistically, with other things," Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas added in an apparent reference to NATO expansion.

Singapore Defence Minister Tony Tan said regional security depended largely on how well China and Washington could develop comfortable ties so that Beijing did not get the impression Washington was pursuing a containment policy.
A leading Chinese academic said many of her compatriots, including officials in the military and foreign ministry, mistrusted the United States but still wanted more engagement.

"There is still quite a bit of suspicion hanging on," said Yuan Ming, an American Studies expert at Beijing University, noting many army officers thought the U.S. military presence in Asia during the Cold War triggered wars in Korea and Vietnam.
